title: Basic Types
summary: TypeScript labels common values as string, number or boolean. It can often work out the label from the value.
introduction: TypeScript labels common values as string, number or boolean. It can often work out the label from the value. Use short examples with names, scores and true-or-false choices. Learn when to add a label and when the checker already knows it.
learningObjectives: Annotate variables with primitive types and recognise when inference already does it
Tell any and unknown apart and explain why unknown is the safe choice
Handle null and undefined explicitly instead of relying on luck

blocks.text: An annotation is a colon and a type after a name: `let title: string`. But you do not need one when the compiler can see the initial value. `let count = 5` gives `count` the type `number` just as surely as writing it out, and the compiler then enforces it for the rest of the variable's life.

blocks.title: infer.ts

blocks.text: Hover over `count` in your editor and it shows `let count: number`. The annotation on `title` is redundant, and most style guides omit it. Inference is not a shortcut that weakens checking: assigning a string to `count` is rejected exactly as if you had annotated it.

blocks.title: npx tsc reassign.ts
blocks.content:
reassign.ts:2:1 - error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

2 count = "six";
  ~~~~~


Found 1 error in reassign.ts:2

blocks.caption: The primitive types
rows: `"hi"`, `'hi'`, or a template literal written in backticks
All three quote styles produce the same type
One type for integers and floats, like JavaScript
Unique keys; rare in application code
Each is its own type under strict mode (see below)

blocks.text: A type does not have to be as wide as `string`. A *literal type* is a single value: the type `"dark"` accepts only the string `"dark"`. Literal types become powerful when you combine them into a union of allowed values, which the [unions lesson](/tutorials/typescript/type-aliases-unions) covers in depth. `const` and `let` infer them differently: a `const` can never change, so its type is the exact literal; a `let` may be reassigned, so the compiler widens it to the primitive.

blocks.title: literal.ts
npx tsc literal.ts
blocks.content:
literal.ts:6:1 - error TS2322: Type '"blue"' is not assignable to type '"dark" | "light"'.

6 theme = "blue";
  ~~~~~


Found 1 error in literal.ts:6

blocks.text: Hovering shows `const state: "active"` but `let mode: string`. Annotating `theme` with two literals turns a typo such as `"blue"` into a compile error instead of a theme that silently falls back to the default. (The message lists the union members in the order the compiler first met them, `"dark"` on line 2 before `"light"` on line 4; the order never affects the meaning.)

`any` switches the checker off for one value: you can call anything on it, pass it anywhere, and the compiler stays silent. It exists for migrating JavaScript and for a few library edge cases, and `JSON.parse` returns it. `unknown` is the opposite: it also accepts every value, but you cannot *do* anything with it until you have proved what it is.

blocks.title: npx tsc unknown.ts
blocks.content:
unknown.ts:3:13 - error TS18046: 'parsed' is of type 'unknown'.

3 console.log(parsed.toUpperCase());
              ~~~~~~


Found 1 error in unknown.ts:3

blocks.text: The fix is a check that the compiler understands, called *narrowing*. Inside the `if`, `parsed` has the type `string` and every string method is available.

blocks.title: unknown-fixed.ts
Common mistake: letting any creep in
blocks.text: Under `strict`, a parameter without an annotation or an inferable value is an error: `function log(message) {}` reports `TS7006: Parameter 'message' implicitly has an 'any' type.` Beginners fix it by writing `message: any`, which makes the error disappear and the checking with it. Write the real type (`message: string`) or, when you truly do not know, `unknown` and narrow it. A project with `any` sprinkled through it has the costs of TypeScript without the benefits.

`void` is the return type of a function that returns nothing useful, such as one that only logs. `never` is the type of a value that cannot exist: the return type of a function that always throws or loops forever, and the type the compiler assigns to a variable once every possibility has been ruled out. You will rarely annotate `never` by hand until the [narrowing lesson](/tutorials/typescript/narrowing), where it powers exhaustiveness checks.
null and undefined under strict mode

In JavaScript any variable can hold `null` or `undefined`, and `Cannot read properties of undefined` is the most common runtime error in the language. With `strict` on (which enables `strictNullChecks`), `null` and `undefined` are separate types that are not assignable to `string`, `number` or anything else unless you say so with a union.

blocks.title: null.ts
npx tsc null.ts
blocks.content:
null.ts:1:5 - error TS2322: Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'string'.

1 let nickname: string = null;
      ~~~~~~~~

null.ts:4:10 - error TS18048: 'text' is possibly 'undefined'.

4   return text.toUpperCase();
           ~~~~


Found 2 errors in the same file, starting at: null.ts:1

blocks.text: Both fixes are explicit. The variable declares that it may hold `null`; the function checks for `undefined` before touching the string. Readers of this code now know exactly where a missing value is possible and where it is not.

blocks.title: null-fixed.ts
When to annotate
blocks.text: Always annotate function parameters (the compiler cannot guess them) and the return types of exported functions (so a change inside the body cannot silently change the contract). Let local variables infer from their initial value. Annotate a variable only when it starts empty or when you want a narrower type than the value suggests, such as `let theme: "light" | "dark"`.

questions.question: What type does the compiler infer for `const answer = 42;`?
questions.explanation: A const can never be reassigned, so its type is the literal 42. A let with the same initialiser would be widened to number.

questions.question: A value of type `unknown` can be passed to a parameter of type `string` without a check.
questions.explanation: unknown is the top type: everything is assignable to it, but it is assignable to nothing except unknown and any until it is narrowed.
